terms: A region where escape velocity exceeds c.
Speed needed to escape a body's gravity.
Boundary of no return around a black hole.
Rs = 2GM/c^2 — radius of a non-rotating event horizon.
Predicted point of infinite curvature at a black hole's centre.
Maximum white dwarf mass, about 1.4 solar masses.
Path white dwarfs follow as they slowly radiate heat away.
Quantum pressure resisting compression of electrons.
Famous nearby white dwarf companion of Sirius.
Explosion of a white dwarf reaching the Chandrasekhar limit.
Hot, dense remnant of a low-mass star.
The hot, dense early state from which the universe expanded.
On large scales the universe is homogeneous and isotropic.
v = H0 d — recession speed scales with distance.
Stretching of light wavelengths from receding sources.
Charge-Coupled Device — silicon array converting photons to charge.
Thermal signal generated even without light.
Vacuum tube amplifying single photons into measurable pulses.
Picture element — one cell of a detector array.
Noise added when reading each pixel out.
The projection of the Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere, the reference circle from which declination is measured.
The celestial equivalent of latitude, measured in degrees north or south of the celestial equator, fixing an object's position together with right ascension.
The apparent yearly path of the Sun across the celestial sphere, tilted about 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator because of Earth's axial tilt.
The angle, measured westward, between an object's current position and the observer's meridian, showing how long since it crossed the meridian.
The celestial equivalent of longitude, measured eastward along the celestial equator in hours, minutes and seconds from the vernal equinox.
Time kept by the apparent motion of the stars; the local sidereal time equals the right ascension of an object currently on the meridian.
A rocky or metallic body, mostly orbiting the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, far smaller than a planet.
An icy body that develops a glowing coma and tails of gas and dust when its orbit brings it close enough to the Sun for the ice to sublimate.
A body orbiting the Sun that is rounded by its own gravity but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood, such as Pluto, Eris and Ceres.
A large, low-density gas or ice giant of the outer Solar System - Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune - with thick atmospheres and ring systems.
A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune's orbit, including dwarf planets such as Pluto, thought to be a source of short-period comets.
A small, dense, rocky planet of the inner Solar System - Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars - with a solid surface and few or no moons.
Cosmological model: universe expanded from a hot, dense state ~13.8 Gyr ago.
Stretching of space itself, increasing distances between galaxies over time.
Brief phase (10^-36 to 10^-32 s) of exponential expansion that smoothed and flattened the universe.
Primordial production of light nuclei (H, He, Li) in the first ~3 minutes.
~380,000 years after the Big Bang, electrons combined with nuclei, freeing photons.
Discredited rival model (Hoyle, Bondi, Gold 1948) where the universe is unchanging on large scales.
Boundary beyond which the universe is unobservable due to finite light travel time.
Universe is homogeneous and isotropic on large scales - the foundation of Lambda-CDM.
Density at which the universe is geometrically flat; ~9 x 10^-27 kg/m^3.
Network of filaments and voids forming the 'cosmic web' on >100 Mpc scales.
Speculative ideas of multiple disconnected universes; outside present observational reach.
Region from which light has had time to reach us; current radius ~46 billion light-years.
Right half of the Moon (Northern Hemisphere) is lit, one week after New Moon.
Earth is between Sun and Moon; the entire near side appears lit.
Left half of the Moon (Northern Hemisphere) is lit, three weeks after New Moon.
Phase when the Moon is between Earth and the Sun; the lit side faces away from Earth.
Time between successive same phases (e.g., New Moon to New Moon): 29.5 days.
Waxing = increasing lit fraction; waning = decreasing lit fraction.
A measure of how bright an object looks from Earth, where smaller numbers are brighter; the naked eye reaches about magnitude 6 in dark skies.
A familiar pattern of stars that is not an official constellation, such as the Plough within Ursa Major or the Summer Triangle spanning three constellations.
A star close enough to the celestial pole that it never sets for a given observer, instead circling the pole above the horizon all night.
One of 88 official regions of the sky defined by the IAU, each containing a recognised star pattern used to navigate the night sky by eye.
The apparent daily east-to-west movement of stars across the sky, caused by the Earth's rotation on its axis from west to east.
The band of constellations along the ecliptic through which the Sun, Moon and planets appear to move as seen from Earth.
Glows from atmospheric atoms excited by solar particles channelled along Earth's field lines.
Huge eruption of plasma and magnetic field into space; can cause geomagnetic storms.
~11-year cycle of sunspot number and magnetic activity; full magnetic cycle is 22 years.
Sudden intense burst of X-ray and UV radiation from magnetic reconnection above sunspots.
Continuous stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun's corona at 400-800 km/s.
Cooler regions (~3,800 K) on the photosphere with strong magnetic fields (~0.3 T).
Each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, so its distance from the Sun varies through the orbit.
A line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the planet moves faster when nearer the Sun at perihelion.
The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis (T squared proportional to a cubed) for bodies orbiting the Sun.
Every mass attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
A measure of how elongated an orbit is; a value of 0 is a perfect circle while values nearer 1 describe increasingly stretched ellipses.
The difference in gravitational pull across a body, mainly from the Moon, which raises two tidal bulges on Earth and drives the cycle of tides.
Hydrogen fusion catalysed by carbon, nitrogen, oxygen; dominant in stars >1.3 solar masses.
Balance between inward gravity and outward pressure; stable stars maintain this state.
Minimum mass of a gas cloud needed for gravitational collapse to overcome thermal pressure.
For main-sequence stars: L is proportional to M to the power ~3.5; massive stars are vastly more luminous.
Contracting cloud of gas and dust accreting mass; precursor to a main-sequence star.
Direct proton-proton fusion to helium; dominant in stars below ~1.3 solar masses (incl. Sun).
Temperature of an equivalent black body radiating the same total flux as the star.
Original system devised at Harvard Observatory, ordering stars by hydrogen-line strength.
Roman numerals I-VII labelling supergiant (I), giant (III), main sequence (V), white dwarf (VII).
Abundance of elements heavier than helium; affects opacity, evolution and population type.
Adds luminosity class to spectral type (e.g., G2V for the Sun); standard since 1943.
OBAFGKM letters based on stellar spectra; correlates strongly with surface temperature.
Photographing a planet by blocking starlight.
NASA mission (2009-2018) finding thousands of transiting planets.
Detecting planets via the lensing of a background star.
Detecting planets by stellar Doppler wobble.
Detecting planets by tiny dips as they cross a star.
Spiral with a central bar — class SB.
Smooth, featureless ellipsoid — class E0 to E7.
Galaxy without a clear shape — class Irr.
Transition class with a disk but no spiral arms — S0.
Disk galaxy with arms — class S.
Colour index — blue minus visual magnitude.
Temperature of a blackbody of equal luminosity.
Scale spaced by powers — used on the L axis.
Energy radiated per second in watts or solar units.
x-axis runs from hot left to cool right.
Diameter of a telescope's primary lens or mirror.
A reflector with a folded light path and a hole in the primary.
A telescope using mirrors to focus light.
A telescope using lenses to focus light.
Ability to distinguish close objects, set by lambda/D.
Fusion of four protons into helium in stellar cores.
Balance between gravity inward and radiation/gas pressure outward.
The phase where a star fuses hydrogen in its core.
A cloud of gas and dust where stars can form.
A contracting cloud not yet fusing hydrogen.
Unit equal to the Sun's mass, about 2 x 10^30 kg.
Dark feature where cool gas absorbs specific wavelengths.
Coolest type, surface below 3,700 K, red.
'Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy Kiss Me' for OBAFGKM.
Hottest type, surface above 30,000 K, blue-white.
Peak wavelength times temperature is a constant.
